description: Article-based learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway.

cards.title: Americans Stopped Joining Things
cards.subtitle: Bowling leagues used to fill evenings. Now people bowl alone.
body: More Americans bowl than ever—but they don't join leagues. They go alone and leave.
Church groups, PTAs, bowling leagues—membership declined across the board.

cards.title: Social Capital Is Hidden Infrastructure
cards.subtitle: Trust and reciprocity make everything else work.
body: Social capital is why you can ask a neighbor to watch your house, why communities solve problems collectively.
When it erodes, institutions do more work with less trust.
cards.takeaway: Social capital makes societies function; its decline has consequences.

cards.title: Generational Shifts Drove Decline
cards.subtitle: The civic generation is dying. Their grandchildren barely join at all.
body: People born before 1945 joined things. Each generation joined less.
A 60-year-old in 1970 was more engaged than a 60-year-old in 1990.
cards.takeaway: Each generation joined organizations less than the one before.

cards.title: Television Changed How We Spend Time
cards.subtitle: Every hour watching TV is an hour not spent with neighbors.
body: TV privatized leisure. Entertainment moved from public spaces to living rooms.
Heavy TV watchers are less likely to attend meetings or trust their neighbors.
cards.takeaway: Television filled hours that used to be social.

cards.title: Suburbs Spread People Out
cards.subtitle: The commute added an hour. That hour came from somewhere.
body:
• Long drives replaced walks
• Garages replaced front porches
• Every 10 min of commuting = 10% less civic participation
Physical design shapes social behavior.
cards.takeaway: Sprawl and commuting reduced time for community engagement.

cards.title: Women Entered the Workforce
cards.subtitle: Women used to run civic infrastructure. Then they got jobs.
body: Women did the civic labor—PTAs, neighborhood networks. When they entered the workforce, that labor didn't redistribute.
It's not that women shouldn't work—it's that society didn't adapt.
cards.takeaway: Women's civic labor decreased without being replaced.

cards.title: Trust in Institutions Collapsed
cards.subtitle: 1964: 77% trusted government. 1994: 19%.
body: Trust in government, media, and corporations all declined.
Low trust creates a vicious cycle. People don't participate in what they don't trust.
cards.takeaway: Institutional trust collapsed, reducing incentives to participate.

cards.title: Informal Connection Declined Too
cards.subtitle: Not just meetings—picnics, card games, dinner parties all dropped.
body: Informal socializing declined even faster than formal membership.
Americans are less likely to know their neighbors' names than a generation ago.
cards.takeaway: Both formal and informal social connections weakened.

cards.title: Democracy Requires Civic Practice
cards.subtitle: You learn to participate by participating.
body: Civic groups are training grounds for running meetings and organizing collective action.
Without practice, citizens become passive. Democracy is a skill that requires exercise.

cards.title: The Internet Didn't Fix It
cards.subtitle: Online connection substitutes for some things—not the ones that matter most.
body: Early optimists thought the internet would rebuild social capital. It didn't.
Online connections are thin—they lack the trust-building of face-to-face interaction.
cards.takeaway: Online connection doesn't fully substitute for in-person community.

cards.title: Inequality Matters
cards.subtitle: Civic participation correlates with income. The connected get more connected.
body: Wealthy people participate more—voting, volunteering, joining. The poor participate less.
Policies reflect the preferences of participants. Social capital inequality reinforces other inequalities.
cards.takeaway: Civic engagement is unequally distributed by class.

cards.title: Rebuilding Takes Intentionality
cards.subtitle: Social capital doesn't return automatically.
body: Reversal requires intentional effort—redesigning communities and institutions to foster connection.
The question isn't whether we can rebuild. It's whether we'll choose to.
cards.takeaway: Social capital must be deliberately rebuilt.
